lessons.name: Rising quartering outgoing
lessons.understand: A target travelling both upward and away on a quartering line. It is not the same task as a straight going-away target, a near-vertical teal, or a flat quarterer, so the source-specific method only applies when this geometry actually matches.

coaching.text: For the specific rising quartering outgoing presentation reviewed in Stage 2, Don Currie/NSCA teaches a vertical intercept to the inside leading edge as a way to avoid target occlusion.
coaching.label: DIRECT

holds: Do not generalise the source's exact hold geometry to different target angles or handedness without adapting the presentation.
Do not treat every rising outgoing target as this quartering presentation.

diagnose.symptom: target disappears behind the gun or the miss is repeatedly behind on the rising quarter
diagnose.label: SHOTSIGHT_HYPOTHESIS
candidate_mechanisms: gun path enters the target's visual line and creates occlusion
late recognition of the combined rising-and-away geometry
late connection before the planned intercept
diagnose.question: On the same no-shot presentation, does target visibility and movement quality improve when you compare line-following with the source-attributed vertical-intercept approach?
diagnose.interpretation: If visibility improves with the source-matched approach, occlusion becomes a stronger coaching hypothesis; if not, retain timing, geometry-reading and connection alternatives.
diagnose.fix: For a presentation that genuinely matches the source geometry, test the attributed vertical-intercept approach without assigning a universal lead value.
diagnose.retest: Change the quartering angle or direction. If the result does not transfer, keep the method presentation-specific.

visual_spec.target: oblique path rising while moving away
visual_spec.warning: Conceptual 2D rehearsal only. Exact hold position, lead and handedness geometry are not universal.

lessons.name: Fast flat quartering away
lessons.understand: A fast quartering-away target with little vertical change around the intended break zone. Speed is a modifier of the quartering geometry, not a separate universal target family.

coaching.text: In the reviewed 'Always Behind' answer, Don Currie/NSCA addresses fast quartering behind-misses with a specific quartering move plus hold/pickup planning and leading-edge visual focus.
coaching.label: DIRECT

holds: This is one coach's source-specific quartering method, not proof that it is the only valid method.
Do not inherit its exact hold/pickup geometry to a different angle, speed or direction.

diagnose.symptom: repeatedly behind on the fast quarterer
diagnose.label: SHOTSIGHT_HYPOTHESIS
candidate_mechanisms: hold/pickup plan leaves too little controlled movement window
diagnose.question: With the break point held constant, does a source-matched hold/pickup plan improve early connection and reduce the repeatable behind miss without increasing correction or rush?
diagnose.interpretation: Improvement would support a timing/connection explanation, but it does not prove a single cause or make the method universally superior.
diagnose.fix: Test the Don Currie/NSCA quartering approach as an attributed option; keep visual priority on target detail/leading edge rather than consciously measuring a fixed lead.
diagnose.retest: Repeat with a changed quartering angle or opposite direction and compare whether the same approach remains controlled.

visual_spec.target: fast, shallow oblique line moving across and away
visual_spec.warning: 2D conceptual rehearsal. Speed, lead and hold distances are not calibrated live-fire values.

lessons.name: Teal near the apex
lessons.understand: A teal-style presentation selected for a break near the top of its rise, where vertical speed is reducing. This is deliberately separate from the under-power rising teal lesson because the timing task and source-attributed method are different.

coaching.text: James Ross/Orvis describes an apex-based method for a single teal, using the top of the flight as the chosen timing context.
coaching.label: DIRECT

holds: Do not present the apex as the universally best place to shoot teal.
Do not merge this apex method with Don Currie's outgoing-under-power teal method; they address different chosen phases.

diagnose.symptom: waits for the top but becomes uncertain or pokes as the teal reaches the apex
diagnose.label: SHOTSIGHT_HYPOTHESIS
candidate_mechanisms: break phase was not committed before the call
shooter reacts to apparent stall instead of executing the chosen apex plan
visual connection is lost during the speed transition
diagnose.question: On repeated identical teals, does pre-committing to the apex-based method reduce hesitation compared with an unplanned 'wait and see' trial?
diagnose.interpretation: A cleaner planned trial would support a process/timing explanation; it would not establish that apex is better than a rising break for this shooter or target.
diagnose.fix: If the presentation and chosen strategy match the source, rehearse the James Ross/Orvis apex method as one attributed option rather than a universal teal rule.
diagnose.retest: Change target speed or compare a deliberate rising break. Preserve whichever phase/method produces the more repeatable process rather than forcing apex.

visual_spec.target: near-vertical rise entering an apex/slowdown zone
visual_spec.warning: Apex is one source-attributed method choice, not a universal teal break point or lead picture.
